headline: Kita is Old Japanese, but its ultimate derivation is unknown.
Okane is just 御 (o-, beautifying prefix) plus 金 (kane, “money”).
Utsukushii was utsukushi, before its ending became しき (shiki) and then the medial k fell out.
Nigai was nigashi in Early Middle Japanese, before its ending was replaced and the medial k fell out.
Ōi is cognate with 大きい (ōkii, “big”), and with Proto-Ryukyuan *opo.
E was we in Middle Chinese 繪, the goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.
Kiru is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kiru, with Ryūkyūan cognates.
Genkan was earlier genkwan; the source notes it was common during the Edo period.
Suzushii may ultimately derive from onomatopoeia; compare 涼む (suzumu, “to cool down”).
Tashika derives from the tashi- element in たしに (tashi ni, “sufficiently; firmly; surely”) plus the suffix か (-ka).
Mukō has two possible sources, both from a nominalization of the verb 向かう (mukau, “to face”).
Sagasu is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *sankasu.
Gaikokujin is, by surface analysis, 外国 (gaikoku, “foreign country”) plus 人 (-jin, “person”).
Umi is theorized to be 大 (ō-, “big”) plus 水 (mi, “water”), though the source finds that problematic.
Hana went /pana/ → /fana/ → /hana/, from Proto-Japonic *pana.
Uriba is 売り (uri, “selling”) plus 場 (ba, “place”), attested since at least 1595.
Onna was womina in Old Japanese, then omina, and the source traces womi1na → womʉna → wonːa → onːa.
Uta is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ota.
Ima is first attested in the Kojiki, and one proposal splits it into i (“this”) plus ma.
Shiraseru is the causative form of the verb 知る (shiru, “to know”).
Byōin is 病 (byō, “illness”) plus 院 (-in, “institution”).
Ryūgakusei is 留学 (ryūgaku) plus 生 (-sei).
Nigeru is from Old Japanese 逃ぐ (nigu), from Proto-Japonic *nink-ai-.
Okashi is 御 (o-, polite prefix) plus 菓子 (kashi, “confection”).
Tsukuru is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *tukoru.
Ichi is from Middle Chinese 一 (ʔiɪt̚), and went itɨ → it͡sɨ → it͡ɕɨ on the way.
Shokudō was jikidō, a refectory in a Buddhist temple, before the Meiji period's kan'on reading of 食.
Jimusho is, by surface analysis, 事務 (jimu) plus 所 (-sho).
Tsugi is a nominalization of the stem of the verb 次ぐ (tsugu, “to follow, to be next; to connect”).
Katachi is 形 (kata, “shape, form”) plus ち (-chi), but the chi element's derivation is unclear.
Kuruma is attested in phonetic spelling as 久流末 (kuruma), and may originally have meant “wheel”.
